analysis.one_liner: Replaced Western wholesale electricity market prices with cost-based caps and ordered crisis overcharge refunds.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have capped Western wholesale power prices at cost and refunded overcharges it said could exceed $6 billion, never received a hearing or vote after being referred to a House subcommittee in April 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: During the 2000-01 Western electricity crisis, this bill would have directed the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to set wholesale electricity rates based on the actual cost of generating power plus a reasonable return, across the Western states, through March 2003. It would have ordered refunds of rates FERC had found unjust going back to June 2000, let states sue in federal court to enforce the caps, and imposed triple penalties on violators. The bill never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Households, businesses, and governments across the Western states that were paying sharply escalating wholesale power costs during the 2000-01 electricity crisis, plus the utilities buying that power. The bill cited a California Independent System Operator estimate that generators overcharged California utilities by more than $6 billion between May 2000 and February 2001, and would have clawed back unjust charges back to June 2000.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Western ratepayers during the power crisis

how_it_helps.text: Capped wholesale electricity rates at cost of service — actual generating costs plus a normal return on capital — for sales across the Western Systems Coordinating Council region, effective within 30 days of enactment and running through March 1, 2003.

Required FERC to refund rates and charges that were not just and reasonable on sales between June 1, 2000 and enactment; the bill's findings cited an estimate of more than $6 billion in overcharges to California utilities and noted FERC's own orders covered only a fraction of them.
Gave states a direct cause of action in federal district court to enforce the caps and win refunds, and exposed violators to civil penalties of three times the amount involved.
Exempted power from generation facilities built after January 1, 2001 from the caps, preserving the profit incentive to build new plants during the shortage.

analysis.who_pays: Merchant power generators and their shareholders, who would have been required to sell at cost-based rates through March 2003 and to refund unjust charges dating back to June 2000. Section 4 also would have required the federal or a state government to guarantee payment for any emergency order requiring a generator to sell or connect power, shifting that financial risk onto taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wholesale power generators and their shareholders

drawbacks.text: Capping prices at cost removes the scarcity signal that normally pushes customers to conserve and investors to build during a shortage. The bill's own findings cited a lack of investment in new generation as a cause of the crisis, and while new plants were exempted from the caps, existing suppliers would have had little reason to add capacity or sell into the region beyond their cost.

The bill would have amended the Federal Power Act so no emergency order could compel a power company to provide electricity or connections unless the federal or a state government fully guaranteed payment, putting governments — and ultimately taxpayers — on the hook for emergency power purchases outside of wartime.

The caps would have expired March 1, 2003 and did nothing about the underlying supply problems the findings acknowledged: drought in the Northwest, high natural gas costs, and rapid population growth in the West.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The caps were temporary, allowed generators a customary 1994-1999 return on capital, and exempted new plants — a design that blunts the standard objection that price controls discourage investment during a shortage. The most significant cost was shifting emergency-order payment risk onto governments. Weighed against the bill's estimate of more than $6 billion in overcharges to California utilities alone, the protections for Western ratepayers appear to have outweighed the costs, though cost-based caps by themselves would not have built a single new power plant or ended the drought.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Air Quality subcommittee, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Jay Inslee introduced the bill on April 4, 2001 during the Western power crisis, with 46 Democratic cosponsors including Minority Leader Richard Gephardt; its findings noted that the governors of California, Oregon, and Washington had asked FERC to impose cost-based rates.

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and on April 25, 2001 to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality. No hearing, markup, or floor action followed.

The bill's findings accused FERC of failing its legal duty to mandate just and reasonable rates, noting the commission had twice found California wholesale rates unjust and unreasonable yet had not imposed cost-based rates in the West.

In June 2001, after months of refusing broader caps, FERC did impose limited price controls on Western wholesale power, but nothing resembling the bill's cost-based rates or region-wide mandatory refunds was ever enacted.
No further action was taken before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and the bill expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wholesale power generators that sold electricity at crisis prices in 2000-01 kept their gains; no cost-based caps or mandatory region-wide refunds were ever imposed, and merchants faced only the narrower, later FERC mitigation orders.

for.name: Jay Inslee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it with a charge that FERC had failed to protect consumers from excessive Western wholesale rates.

for.name: 46 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Minority Leader Richard Gephardt and senior Californians such as Nancy Pelosi and Henry Waxman.

for.name: Governors of California, Oregon, and Washington
for.what_they_did: Wrote to FERC's chairman and commissioners on March 9, 2001 requesting cost-of-service-based rates for the Western region.

against.name: Billy Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired referred the bill to subcommittee on April 25, 2001 and took no further action on it; no markup or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Joe Barton
against.role: Chair, Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality
against.what_they_did: The subcommittee where the bill sat took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
against.what_they_did: Had found California wholesale rates unjust and unreasonable twice but declined to impose cost-of-service-based rates in the West, which the bill's findings called a failure of its legal duty.

against.name: Merchant power generators
against.what_they_did: Opposed Western wholesale price caps and retroactive refunds during the crisis, arguing controls would discourage investment and worsen the shortage.

sides.party_line_note: All 46 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; the Republican-run Energy and Commerce Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have forced them to sell electricity in the Western market at cost plus a regulated return through March 2003 and to refund unjust charges back to June 2000 — directly targeting the profits of the roughly $6 billion in overcharges the bill cited. Their interest in the bill ran squarely against Western ratepayers.

industries.industry: Investor-owned electric utilities and power buyers
industries.note: Utilities and public agencies buying wholesale power would have paid cost-based rates and recovered charges found unjust, easing the financial squeeze that helped push California's largest utility toward bankruptcy during the crisis.
